ideas: Rejected verification and induction alike. No number of white swans verifies 'all swans are white', but one black swan refutes it, so the logic of science is falsification.
Demarcation: what separates science from pseudo-science is not proof but risk. A scientific theory forbids things, so it can fail. Marxism and psychoanalysis explained everything and forbade nothing.
Theories are never proved, only corroborated so far. Knowledge grows by conjectures and refutations.
The Open Society and Its Enemies, written in exile during the war, attacks Plato, Hegel and Marx as historicists whose claim to know history's laws licenses tyranny.
The paradox of tolerance: unlimited tolerance leads to the disappearance of tolerance, since the intolerant will not reciprocate.
works: The Logic of Scientific Discovery; Conjectures and Refutations; The Open Society and Its Enemies.

people.one: Thought must resist the systems it cannot help building.
ideas: Negative dialectics: the concept never exhausts the object, and philosophy's task is to keep faith with what falls outside it rather than to complete a system.
With Horkheimer, the culture industry: mass culture is industrially produced, standardised, and works to make people fit for the order that produces it.
Minima Moralia, written in exile, is philosophy in aphorisms about damaged life. 'There is no right life in the wrong one.'
Also a trained composer, a student of Alban Berg, and a serious music theorist who championed Schoenberg and attacked jazz.
His 'to write poetry after Auschwitz is barbaric' is almost always quoted without the qualifications he later added.
Confronted by protesting students in 1969 who found his refusal to endorse direct action a betrayal; he died of a heart attack months later.
works: Dialectic of Enlightenment; Negative Dialectics; Minima Moralia; Aesthetic Theory.

people.one: Existence precedes essence. We are what we make of ourselves.
ideas: For a paper knife, essence precedes existence: the design comes before the object. For us there is no designer and no blueprint, so we exist first and define ourselves after.
Consciousness is a nothingness, a hole in being, which is why it can never coincide with itself as a table coincides with itself.
We are condemned to be free: not free to choose our situation, but unable to avoid choosing how to take it up. Even refusing to choose is a choice.
Bad faith is fleeing that freedom by pretending to be a thing with a fixed nature: the waiter playing at being a waiter, the coward telling himself he was born that way.
Others turn me into an object by looking at me, which is why 'hell is other people' in No Exit is about the gaze, not about company.
Turned to Marxism after the war and tried to fuse it with existentialism, arguing that freedom is always exercised within material conditions.
Refused the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964, on the ground that a writer should not let himself be turned into an institution.
Lifelong partner of Simone de Beauvoir, in an open relationship they both wrote about.
works: Being and Nothingness; Existentialism is a Humanism; Nausea; No Exit; Critique of Dialectical Reason.

q.t: Man is condemned to be free; because once thrown into the world, he is responsible for everything he does.

people.one: Politics is what happens when plural people act together in public.
ideas: The Origins of Totalitarianism argues that Nazism and Stalinism were a new form of rule, not merely extreme tyranny, resting on ideology, terror and the atomisation of mass society.

In The Human Condition she distinguishes labour (which sustains life), work (which builds a durable world) and action (which discloses who we are among others), and argues that modernity has collapsed the third into the first two.
'Natality', the fact that new beginnings keep entering the world, is her counterweight to Heidegger's being-toward-death.

Reporting on Eichmann's trial, she coined 'the banality of evil' to describe a functionary who did not think rather than a monster. The phrase was widely misread as excusing him, and cost her friendships for life.
Studied under Heidegger, who was also her lover, and under Jaspers; fled Germany in 1933 and France in 1941. Resisted the label 'philosopher', preferring political theorist.
works: The Origins of Totalitarianism; The Human Condition; Eichmann in Jerusalem; The Life of the Mind.

people.one: Ethics comes before ontology. The other person makes a claim on me.
ideas: Introduced Husserl and Heidegger to France, then argued that the whole tradition, in asking first about Being, subordinates the other person to a system that comprehends them.
The face of the other resists being turned into a concept. It commands, before any argument, 'thou shalt not kill'.
Responsibility is not chosen and not symmetrical: I am responsible for the other, and even for the other's responsibility, without expecting return.
Spent the war in a prisoner-of-war camp as a French soldier; most of his Lithuanian family were murdered in the Holocaust, which is the unstated pressure behind the work.
works: Totality and Infinity; Otherwise than Being; Time and the Other.

people.one: We are not minds attached to bodies. We are bodies that perceive.
ideas: Against both intellectualism and empiricism: perception is not a mind interpreting sensations, nor a body receiving stimuli, but a bodily engagement with a world already meaningful.
The lived body is not an object among objects. It is the point of view from which there are objects at all, and I know where my hand is without looking.
Drew heavily on Gestalt psychology and on cases of neurological damage, treating empirical work as philosophically load-bearing.
Perception is always perspectival and never complete, so ambiguity is not a defect to be cleared up but the condition of having a world.
Broke with Sartre over the Korean War and Soviet labour camps, and edited Les Temps Modernes until then.
Prefigured a great deal of later embodied and enactive cognitive science.
works: Phenomenology of Perception; The Structure of Behavior; The Visible and the Invisible.

people.one: One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.
ideas: The Second Sex (1949) applies existentialist categories to sex: femininity is not a nature but a situation, produced and enforced.
Woman has been constituted as the Other, defined relative to man as the norm, so that 'he is the Subject, he is the Absolute; she is the Other'.

Two volumes: the first on biology, psychoanalysis and history, the second on lived experience from childhood to old age. It sold twenty-two thousand copies in its first week and was placed on the Vatican's index.
The Ethics of Ambiguity is arguably a better worked-out existentialist ethics than Sartre managed, grounding obligation in the fact that my freedom requires the freedom of others.
Also wrote a serious philosophical treatment of ageing, The Coming of Age, at a time when nobody else did.
works: The Second Sex; The Ethics of Ambiguity; The Mandarins; The Coming of Age.

q.t: One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.

people.one: There is no sharp line between analytic and synthetic, and no belief faces experience alone.
ideas: 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951) took apart logical positivism from the inside. The first dogma is the analytic-synthetic distinction, which he argued cannot be defined without circling through synonymy and back again.

The second is reductionism, the idea that each statement has its own confirming experiences. Instead our beliefs 'face the tribunal of experience' as a corporate body: a web of belief, with logic and mathematics at the centre and observation at the edge, and any statement can be held true if we revise enough elsewhere.
Ontological relativity and the indeterminacy of translation: 'gavagai' might mean rabbit, or undetached rabbit part, and no amount of behavioural evidence decides.
'To be is to be the value of a bound variable' made ontology a question about what our best theories quantify over.
Naturalised epistemology: give up the search for foundations and study knowing as a chapter of psychology.
works: Two Dogmas of Empiricism; Word and Object; From a Logical Point of View; Ontological Relativity.

people.one: Brought logical positivism to Britain, at twenty-four.
ideas: Went to Vienna in 1933, sat in on the Circle, and wrote Language, Truth and Logic in 1936.
Argued that metaphysical statements are literally senseless, being neither analytic nor verifiable.
Emotivism: moral judgements express feelings and seek to influence, rather than state facts. 'Stealing is wrong' says no more than 'stealing' in a tone of disapproval.
Later conceded the book was almost entirely wrong, while remaining glad he wrote it.
works: Language, Truth and Logic; The Problem of Knowledge.

people.one: Saying something is usually doing something.
ideas: Speech act theory: 'I promise', 'I name this ship', 'I do' are not descriptions that can be true or false but performances that can succeed or misfire.
Distinguished the locutionary act (what is said), the illocutionary act (what is done in saying it) and the perlocutionary effect (what it brings about).
Argued that the vast stock of distinctions embedded in ordinary language has survived because it is useful, and is a better starting point than a philosopher's invented terminology.
Sense and Sensibilia dismantles the argument from illusion and the sense-datum theory.
works: How to Do Things with Words; Sense and Sensibilia; Philosophical Papers.

people.one: Life has no given meaning, and the answer is to live anyway.
ideas: The absurd is not a property of the world or of us but the confrontation between the human demand for meaning and the world's silence.
'There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide.' His answer is no: suicide and the leap of faith both dissolve the tension rather than living it.
Sisyphus, condemned to roll his rock forever, is the absurd hero because he is conscious and does not consent to despair. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.
The Rebel argues that rebellion affirms a value and therefore has limits, which is where it parts from revolution that licenses murder. The argument ended his friendship with Sartre.
Rejected the existentialist label. Nobel Prize in Literature 1957, at forty-four. Killed in a car crash three years later with an unused train ticket in his pocket.
works: The Myth of Sisyphus; The Stranger; The Plague; The Rebel.

q.t: One must imagine Sisyphus happy.

people.one: Restarted virtue ethics, and made intention a philosophical subject.
ideas: 'Modern Moral Philosophy' (1958) argued that the concepts of moral obligation and duty are survivals from a law conception of ethics that has lost its lawgiver, and are therefore incoherent without it. She urged a return to Aristotle, and coined 'consequentialism' as a term of criticism.
Intention: what makes an event an action is that a certain sense of the question 'why?' applies to it, one that asks for a reason rather than a cause.
Wittgenstein's student, literary executor and translator of the Philosophical Investigations.
Publicly protested Oxford's honorary degree for Truman in 1956, on the ground that he had ordered the deliberate killing of civilians.
works: Intention; Modern Moral Philosophy; An Introduction to Wittgenstein's Tractatus.

people.one: Justice is what we would choose if we did not know who we would be.
ideas: A Theory of Justice (1971) revived normative political philosophy, which had been widely declared dead by the positivists.

The original position: parties choose principles for their society behind a veil of ignorance that hides their class, talents, race, sex and conception of the good. Whatever they choose is fair, because nobody can rig it in their own favour.

They would choose, first, equal basic liberties for all, and second, that social and economic inequalities be attached to offices open to all and arranged to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged, the difference principle.
Liberty has lexical priority: you cannot trade basic freedoms for economic gains.

Later, in Political Liberalism, asked how a just society is possible when citizens hold irreconcilable but reasonable comprehensive doctrines, and answered with overlapping consensus and public reason.
Fought in the Pacific in the Second World War, and refused most honours afterwards.
works: A Theory of Justice; Political Liberalism; The Law of Peoples.

people.one: Between Popper and Kuhn: research programmes, progressive or degenerating.
ideas: Imprisoned in Stalinist Hungary, fled after 1956, and became Popper's most interesting critic.
The unit of appraisal is not a single theory but a research programme, with a hard core held immune by decision and a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses that absorb refutations.

A programme is progressive if its modifications predict novel facts that are then found, and degenerating if they only patch failures after the event. That keeps Popper's rationality without his naive falsificationism.
Proofs and Refutations shows mathematics itself growing by conjecture, counterexample and the reworking of concepts, using the history of Euler's polyhedron formula.
works: Proofs and Refutations; The Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes.

people.one: Science alternates between routine puzzle-solving and revolution.
ideas: A physicist who, while teaching a history course, tried to understand Aristotle's physics and realised it was not bad Newton but a coherent scheme with different questions.
Normal science works inside a paradigm, an accepted framework of theory, method and exemplary problem-solutions. Most scientists spend their lives solving puzzles it defines.
Anomalies accumulate, a crisis develops, and a new paradigm replaces the old in a shift that is not a simple accumulation of truth.
Paradigms are incommensurable: terms shift meaning across the divide, and there is no neutral observation language to adjudicate, because observation is theory-laden.
Structure is among the most cited academic books ever written, and Kuhn spent much of his later life resisting the relativist readings of it.
works: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions; The Copernican Revolution; The Essential Tension.

people.one: There is no single scientific method. Anything goes.
ideas: Argued from case studies, especially Galileo, that every methodological rule has been broken at some point by scientists who turned out to be right, and that progress required breaking it.
'Anything goes' is not advice but the only rule that survives the historical record, offered with deliberate provocation.
Counter-induction: sometimes you should develop hypotheses inconsistent with well-established facts, since the facts may be artefacts of the theory being challenged.
Held that science should not have a privileged place in a free society, a position most philosophers of science rejected and which he pressed anyway.
works: Against Method; Science in a Free Society; Farewell to Reason.

people.one: Difference is prior to identity, and becoming to being.
ideas: Argued that the tradition has always subordinated difference to identity, treating things as different from something. He wants difference in itself.

Wrote a counter-canon of thinkers the mainstream marginalised, Lucretius, Spinoza, Hume, Nietzsche, Bergson, describing his early monographs as taking authors from behind and giving them monstrous children.
With Félix Guattari, Anti-Oedipus attacked psychoanalysis for confining desire to the family triangle, and proposed desire as productive rather than lacking.
The rhizome, against the tree: a model of knowledge with no root, no hierarchy and any point connectable to any other.
Philosophy is not reflection or communication but the creation of concepts.
works: Difference and Repetition; Anti-Oedipus and A Thousand Plateaus (with Guattari); What Is Philosophy?

people.one: Knowledge and power produce each other, and produce us.
ideas: Took Nietzsche's genealogy and applied it to institutions: madness, medicine, punishment, sexuality. Each history shows a category we take as natural being assembled at a particular moment.
Power/knowledge: power is not only repressive but productive. It makes subjects, categories and truths. And every field of knowledge opens a field of control.

Discipline and Punish opens with a public execution and, three pages later, a prison timetable, arguing that punishment moved from the body to the soul, and that Bentham's panopticon is the model of modern power: visibility that makes people police themselves.
The History of Sexuality rejects the 'repressive hypothesis'. The Victorians did not silence sex, they produced an enormous discourse about it, and made it the truth of the self.
Biopower: the modern state governs populations, birth rates, health, life itself, rather than merely threatening death.
Late work turned to the care of the self and ancient practices of freedom. Died of AIDS in 1984.
works: Madness and Civilization; The Order of Things; Discipline and Punish; The History of Sexuality.

people.one: Modern moral language is the wreckage of a tradition it no longer has.
ideas: After Virtue (1981) opens with a thought experiment: imagine science destroyed and later reconstructed from fragments, so people use its terms without the framework that made them intelligible. That, he argues, is the state of our moral vocabulary.

Without Aristotle's teleology, a conception of what humans are for, moral claims lose their ground, and disagreement becomes interminable. Emotivism is then a correct description of what moral talk has become.
Rebuilt virtue ethics through practices, which have internal goods and standards of excellence, the narrative unity of a human life, and the traditions that carry both.

Rationality itself is tradition-constituted: there is no view from nowhere from which to adjudicate between rival traditions, but traditions can still be compared by how well each handles its own crises.
works: After Virtue; Whose Justice? Which Rationality?; Dependent Rational Animals.

people.one: Reason survives, in the structure of communication itself.
ideas: Broke with Horkheimer and Adorno's pessimism. Instrumental reason is not all of reason; there is also communicative rationality, oriented to reaching understanding rather than to control.
Anyone who makes a claim in earnest implicitly commits to redeeming it with reasons if challenged. That commitment is the normative core he builds on.
Discourse ethics: a norm is valid only if all affected could accept it in an unconstrained discussion where only the force of the better argument counts.
The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere traces the rise of a bourgeois public of coffee houses and journals, and its later hollowing by mass media and public relations.
Defended modernity as an unfinished project against the postmodernists, and has intervened publicly for fifty years on German memory, European integration and bioethics.
works: The Theory of Communicative Action; The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere; Between Facts and Norms.

people.one: Meaning is never fully present, and every text undoes its own hierarchy.
ideas: Deconstruction is not demolition. It shows that a text's governing opposition (speech over writing, presence over absence, nature over culture) is unstable, and that the privileged term depends on the one it excludes.

The metaphysics of presence: the tradition has treated meaning as something fully present in the moment of speech, with writing as a fallen copy. He argues the features blamed on writing are true of language as such.
Différance, spelled with an a and audible only in writing, names both differing and deferring: a sign means by its difference from others and by endlessly postponing a final meaning.
'There is nothing outside the text' is not the claim that reality is unreal but that there is no access to meaning from outside all contexts.
Later work on hospitality, forgiveness, the gift and justice, which he called undeconstructible.
A Cambridge honorary degree in 1992 was opposed by an open letter from analytic philosophers, which captures how deep the two streams' mutual incomprehension ran.
works: Of Grammatology; Writing and Difference; Speech and Phenomena; Specters of Marx.

people.one: Justice is about how holdings came about, not how they are distributed.
ideas: Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) was written as a reply to Rawls, and opened by conceding that political philosophers must now work within Rawls' theory or explain why not.

Entitlement theory: a distribution is just if everyone is entitled to what they hold, through just original acquisition or just voluntary transfer, plus rectification of past injustice. There is no separate pattern to match.

The Wilt Chamberlain argument: start from any distribution you consider just, let a million people each freely pay a quarter to watch him play, and the pattern is destroyed by nothing but voluntary acts. Preserving a pattern therefore requires continuous interference with free exchange.
Taxation of earnings from labour is on a par with forced labour.
Only a minimal state, limited to protection against force, theft and fraud and to enforcing contracts, is justified.
The experience machine argument against hedonism: most people would not plug into a machine giving perfect simulated pleasure, so pleasure is not all we want.
works: Anarchy, State, and Utopia; Philosophical Explanations; The Examined Life.

people.one: Names refer through causal chains, and some necessary truths are discovered.
ideas: Published a completeness proof for modal logic, giving possible-world semantics, while still a teenager.

Naming and Necessity (1970, delivered as lectures without notes) attacked the description theory of names: 'Aristotle' does not abbreviate 'the teacher of Alexander', since Aristotle might never have taught him and would still have been Aristotle.

Names are rigid designators, picking out the same individual in every possible world where that individual exists, and reference is fixed by an initial baptism and passed down a causal-historical chain of use.

Prised apart necessity, an metaphysical notion, from the a priori, an epistemic one. 'Water is H2O' is necessarily true if true at all, yet was discovered by experiment: a necessary a posteriori truth. And there are contingent a priori truths too.
This made essentialism respectable again in analytic philosophy after decades of positivist hostility.
Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language proposed a sceptical paradox about rule-following that is now discussed as 'Kripkenstein', whoever it belongs to.
works: Naming and Necessity; Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language; Semantical Considerations on Modal Logic.

edges.note: Twenty years in the Academy, then a lifetime of disagreement with it.
Augustine read 'the books of the Platonists' in Latin and found in them everything but the Incarnation.
Boethius' translation of the Isagoge handed the medieval world the problem of universals.
For six centuries, Boethius' logical translations were the Latin West's entire Aristotle.
The Incoherence of the Philosophers, answered by The Incoherence of the Incoherence.
Aquinas cites him simply as 'the Commentator'.
The real distinction between essence and existence.
Cited throughout as 'Rabbi Moses'.
